provenance: Telephone call, 2026-09-13, Larry's son asking the four cold van questions from the head of the interview guide, exactly as written and with nothing else said or shown first, and typing Larry's answers as he spoke them. This answer is to: "Who was the officer in charge of your van?" Raw capture: research/interviews/breakfast-questions.md, annotated in place under each question.
text: I don't think we had one. I think Sargeant Chapman was in charge of it. I never seen officers in there. Officers left us alone completely other then flying with them.
researchNotes: First of four questions asked cold: no name, rank, number or unit supplied, nothing shown. The question presupposed an officer, and he rejected the presupposition: no officer in charge of the van, Chapman ran it, and officers were met only in the air. Against the October 1964 item in research/units/18th-aod-stars-and-stripes-1964.md, THIS DOES NOT MATCH the printed role, and it must never be written up as confirmation. Nor does it undo the unit identification, which rests on three surnames appearing together, not on roles. Readings, none preferred: the printed role was a paper one, not someone on shift; that officer had moved on before Larry joined the van crew (the item falls in what he describes as his Nha Trang months); or his van is not the printed one. He named no officer. "Other then flying with them" fits how he remembers the one officer he has named from his unit: a pilot he flew with. "Sargeant" is his son's keystrokes, not a spelling Larry chose. HIS SON'S NOTES ON THE CALL, given the same evening in answer to follow-up questions (the typist's observations, not Larry's words): he seemed not to know who ran the van, since officers weren't there, and may have answered with a guess. Weigh "I think Sargeant Chapman was in charge of it" accordingly. It is hedged in the words themselves ("I think"), and his son heard it as uncertain.
